evidence.claim: Model risk score 0.90. 74% of the alarms the bank cleared scored at or above 0.85 against 9% of confirmed fraud, so a score this high is evidence AGAINST fraud rather than for it. The weight is damped from the measured value because every cleared case in the history was selected from a high score to begin with

The identity record marks this device New for the account. 83% of cleared alarms had a New device against 18% of confirmed fraud: on its own a new device is the signature of a cardholder who has just bought a phone, not of a compromise

Device profile 'Windows | other | chrome 61.0 | 1280x720' is shared with 2 other card(s) inside the 30-day window, across 3 customer(s). Named here because policy R6 requires the shared element to be identified; it carries no weight in the probability, because device sharing at this scale measured no better than chance against the bank's closed cases

This exact amount ($99.92) has been charged to this card 13 times across 4 distinct months under the same product code, a median of 27 days apart. That is the cadence of a subscription, and policy R7 forbids blocking on it
The bank has 3 confirmed-fraud case(s) already closed on this card (CC-5026, CC-2860, CC-2011), pattern(s): card_not_present_fraud, out_of_region_use

External email-domain intelligence classifies 'verizon.net' as an address tied to a paid internet, cable or phone subscription, which means a billing relationship and a credit check stand behind it. Measured against the bank's closed cases that points away from fraud (log-likelihood ratio -1.24). The domain is in the transaction; what kind of domain it is, is not -- that is the one piece of evidence here the institution does not own.

The 5 closed cases whose transaction most resembles this one (CC-0757, CC-3020, CC-0635, CC-3012, CC-4375) closed as 1 confirmed fraud (card not present new device) and 4 cleared. Cited as memory; it carries no weight, because it resembles on the same features the score already uses

Connected components place this card in the graph's giant device-sharing component (2,500 cards). Transitive device sharing percolates at every threshold tested, so membership is not evidence of a ring and carries no weight here; it is recorded because policy R6 asks for the shared element to be named.

Policy rule R7: Disputed but legitimate: R7. Disputed but legitimate. When the customer disputes a charge that matches their own recurring pattern (same merchant, same amount, monthly), recommend `CREATE_CASE`, `VERIFY_WITH_CUSTOMER`, and `WARN_CUSTOMER`. Do not block.

Policy rule R6: Shared origin: R6. Shared origin. When several cards show fraud from the same device profile, the same billing region, or the same recipient email in one window, name the shared element, recommend `CREATE_CASE` and `FILE_REPORT`, and `MONITOR_CONNECTED_CARDS` for every card that shares it.

case.summary: The risk score on card C07987-K2 for a $99.92 online transaction on 2016-12-01 was 0.90, and the identity record marked the device as New for the account. Against fraud, the bank has 3 confirmed-fraud case(s) already closed on this card (CC-5026, CC-2860, CC-2011), pattern(s): card_not_present_fraud, out_of_region_use, and external email-domain intelligence classified 'verizon.net' with a log-likelihood ratio of -1.24. For the cardholder, the exact amount ($99.92) had been charged to this card 13 times across 4 distinct months under the same product code, a median of 27 days apart, and 2 other card(s) transacted through the same device profile in the window. The case (CC-0757, CC-3020, CC-0635, CC-3012, CC-4375) was assessed as legitimate at probability 0.11, undocumented, with exposure of $0.00.
